comparison: Both strongly support that rapamycin activates TRPM8, with convergent evidence from calcium imaging, patch-clamp, and genetic knockout experiments. OpenEval emphasizes the dose-response characterization and EC50 values, while peer reviewers highlight the 'solid functional evidence' and 'valuable findings' with explicit affirmation from all reviewers.

Both support direct binding mechanism through inside-out patch experiments and kinetic evidence. OpenEval focuses on membrane-delimited activation and concentration comparisons, while peer reviewers note 'extensive effort' and 'solid evidence' for direct interaction, with Reviewer 3 emphasizing that rapamycin activates TRPM8 directly rather than through accessory proteins.

Both support the NMR methodology for identifying binding epitopes, though with some reservations. OpenEval notes technical variability (2 of 3 replicates showed clear signals), while peer reviewers acknowledge the method as 'intriguing and supportive' but note 'further validation is needed' (Reviewer 1) and improvements in presentation quality (Reviewer 3).

Both support the mutagenesis evidence for a distinct rapamycin binding site. OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from mutagenesis, NMR, and docking while acknowledging allosteric effects cannot be fully excluded. Peer reviewers accept the findings with appropriate caveats about molecular docking limitations, with Reviewer 1 noting authors are 'appropriately careful' about model interpretation.

Both support the kinetic characterization and Type I agonist classification. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of activation/deactivation kinetics and synergy data, while peer reviewers accept this characterization without question as part of the functional evidence base.

Both support the finding that D802A mutation's effect on rapamycin sensitivity is independent of calcium binding. OpenEval emphasizes the calcium uncaging experiments distinguishing icilin from rapamycin, while peer reviewers accept this mechanistic distinction without challenge.

Both strongly support the structure-activity relationship findings showing the cyclohexanol moiety's importance. OpenEval emphasizes systematic SAR data and convergence with docking predictions, while Reviewer 2 specifically highlights this as 'very impressive' work showing detailed dissection of binding versus activation determinants.

Both support the competitive binding evidence from everolimus experiments. OpenEval focuses on selective inhibition of rapamycin but not menthol responses, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the impressive dissection showing the shared portion is for binding while the hydroxyl group is for activation.

Both support the distinction between TRPM8-mediated and TRPA1-mediated menthol responses. OpenEval emphasizes the high overlap (92±7%) between rapamycin-insensitive menthol responders and cinnamaldehyde responders, while peer reviewers accept this as evidence for rapamycin's superior selectivity as a TRPM8 tool.

Both support the discussion of therapeutic implications comparing EC50 values with clinical plasma concentrations. OpenEval notes appropriate caution about local tissue concentrations, while peer reviewers accept this speculation as appropriately framed, with the editor and Reviewer 2 noting potential 'previously unknown physiological effects or therapeutic mechanisms.'

Both address structure-activity relationships. OpenEval R11 focuses on comparing cyclohexanol (TRPM8) versus macrolactam ring (immunosuppression) determinants, while peer R7 emphasizes the impressive dissection of binding versus activation. Minimal claim overlap (C128) but related structural themes.

Both support the comparative analysis with TRPML1. OpenEval presents this as straightforward bioinformatics noting distinct binding mechanisms, while peer reviewers specifically requested this comparison (Reviewer 2) and acknowledged it was addressed in revision.

Both support the recommendation to use everolimus instead of rapamycin in mTOR studies. OpenEval frames this as a logical practical application, while peer reviewers accept it without question, with Reviewer 1 noting it reminds researchers that 'specific' is only meaningful in context of what has been tested.

Both address therapeutic context. OpenEval R18 supports C126 about therapeutic implications with appropriate citations, while peer R10 accepts broader therapeutic speculation about rapamycin's physiological effects. Minimal overlap but related themes about clinical relevance.

OpenEval supports the bioinformatics analysis of binding site conservation and structural comparison with TRPV1 (C133-C137). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific evolutionary/structural context claims.

OpenEval supports background claims about rapamycin (C1-C8, C35-C43) as well-established with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not comment on uncontroversial background information.

OpenEval supports background claims about TRPM8 structure and function (C10-C11, C17-C34) as well-established with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not comment on standard background material.

OpenEval supports the TRPM8 agonist classification scheme (C75-C78) from authors' prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this framework is implicitly accepted when reviewers accept the Type I agonist classification in peer R5.

OpenEval supports the summary of major findings (C144-C146) with appropriate caution about speculative therapeutic implications. Peer R1 includes C144 but focuses on the core activation finding rather than the summary nature of these claims.

OpenEval rates C138 as UNCERTAIN, noting the speculation about avoiding side effects is unsupported by evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific forward-looking claim about drug development.
